Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Woman stranded in Spain after UK’s eVisa system mistakes her for twin sister Nidia Webb, who is legally settled in UK, falls foul of ‘known issue’ with Home Office’s digitised immigration process Kevin Rawlinson Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.57 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A woman who is legally settled in the UK was left stranded at a Spanish airport after the Home Office’s post-Brexit visa system mixed her up with her twin sister. Nidia Webb fell foul of what she was told was a “known issue” with the eVisa, which was brought in as part of the government’s drive to digitise the UK’s immigration system but has faced problems that have caused concern for thousands of people. Politico reported that Webb, who has lived in the UK for eight years, was told at the departure gate she would not be able to board her flight home. “My digital settled status had become linked to my identical twin sister’s details rather than my own, meaning my status could not be properly matched to my identity,” she said. “I was informed that this is a known technical issue affecting some twins within the Home Office system.” Webb said Home Office staff promised her over the phone the problem would be fixed, though a confirmation email was then sent to her sister instead of to her. “I had no idea the issue had been corrected until I was allowed to board my flight home,” Webb said. “Had I not spent hours on the phone trying to resolve the matter, I have no idea how long I could have remained stranded abroad.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status. As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. “In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.” The Home Office indicated the problem Webb encountered had since been fixed and that staff would contact her directly. Serious concerns have been expressed about the eVisa system. In July 2025, the Guardian reported up to 200,000 people who had lived in the UK legally for decades were at risk of being caught up in a Windrush-style scandal because the Home Office was unable to get in touch with them to transfer their old immigration documents to the new digital system. Monique Hawkins, the acting chief executive of the immigration campaign group the3million, said it had seen previous cases similar to Webb’s, adding that it highlighted vulnerabilities in the system and it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status”. She told Politico the eVisa rollout had been “rushed”, adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Home Office Brexit European Union Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania Footage shows clash with French police on beach as dinghy tries to leave for UK Government could pay higher rents to spread asylum accommodation across UK Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022 Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire Judge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme Is Reform UK’s plan to use the navy to stop small boat crossings feasible? US lawmakers from both parties condemned the restrictions, while SpaceX pointed to US government control of military-grade Starshield. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 15, 2026, 4:16 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied President Volodymyr Zelensky arrives to meet with Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham at 10 Downing Street, in central London, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Henry Nicholls / POOL / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip President Volodymyr Zelensky said Starlink satellite communications were intentionally restricted during massive Russian attacks on Ukraine, questioning explanations that the disruption was caused by technical problems. Speaking in an exclusive interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said the restrictions undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, defend its energy infrastructure and protect civilians. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The Ukrainian president said the disruption began around 1 a.m., as Russia launched another wave of missiles and drones against Ukraine. “I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky said when Morgan asked whether the restrictions were deliberate. Advertisement “We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added. His remarks came as Ukrainian officials confirmed speed restrictions affecting military communications and US lawmakers from both parties condemned the disruption, warning that it could endanger Ukrainian civilians and benefit Russia. ‘People are dying because of his decision’ Zelensky said Ukrainian forces immediately contacted SpaceX, American military commanders and other US partners after discovering the overnight disruptions. American officials had attributed the intelligence-sharing problems to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the disruptions reportedly continued during subsequent attacks. Other Topics of Interest ‘Putin Is Laughing’ – Zelensky Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal a Victory for Moscow In an interview with Piers Morgan, Zelensky described Trump’s Russian diesel deal as a tactical victory for Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washingt Starlink, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in Ukraine’s defense against Russian Shahed drones, including interceptor drones that use satellite communications to reach incoming targets. “It’s not about just attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s not about attack. It’s also about defending the lives,” Zelensky told Morgan. Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the decision as a serious mistake. Advertisement “I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said. He nevertheless warned of the consequences. “People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said, cautioning that further casualties could follow if Russian attacks continued while Starlink remained restricted. He appealed directly for the restoration of normal service. “I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know, but we are asking... to switch on,” he said. US lawmakers condemn restrictions as potentially aiding Russia The tightening of Ukraine’s satellite communications access drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, with lawmakers questioning the consequences of limiting critical defensive capabilities during active Russian attacks. The Congressional Ukraine Caucus, whose co-chairs include Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley and Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, issued a joint warning. “We are alarmed by reports from Ukraine that US intelligence and Starlink support are being withheld, putting innocent civilians and American citizens in Ukraine at the mercy of Russian attacks,” the lawmakers said. Advertisement The caucus said Washington must continue providing intelligence to protect civilians and stressed that US allies pay for Ukraine’s Starlink access. “Restrictions that put civilians in harm’s way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress,” the lawmakers declared. Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina also publicly challenged Musk, warning that intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself could be construed as helping a mass murderer. Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska criticized the administration’s handling of intelligence-sharing and Starlink access, arguing that reducing such support effectively aided Russia’s invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian cities. Their objections underscored concern among Ukraine’s Republican supporters that the restrictions could weaken Kyiv’s defensive capabilities at a critical moment. Democratic lawmakers also raised questions about the humanitarian and strategic consequences of restricting systems on which Ukrainian troops and civilians depend. Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer of Maryland issued one of the strongest statements, warning that the restrictions could leave more Ukrainian civilians exposed to Russian attacks. Advertisement In an official statement , Hoyer said that if Trump administration officials were involved, it would represent a “heinous act of betrayal” of Ukraine and a fellow democracy under attack. He called for full Starlink access to be restored, arguing that Washington should help Ukraine win rather than tip the scales in Putin’s favor. European allies also joined the criticism. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski confronted Musk on X, questioning whether the billionaire was using satellite communications as a political instrument. “Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski wrote, warning that European customers were watching. Musk points to US military and Trump Musk responded by distinguishing between commercial Starlink and Starshield, the military-grade satellite service. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk wrote on X. He said decisions about operational limits were ultimately made by the US military and the president. Musk maintained that commercial Starlink service could be used for civilian and defensive purposes but should not support offensive military operations. A senior US official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration had not been involved in imposing the restrictions. Ukrainian officials remained suspicious that the move was connected to Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil facilities. The conflicting accounts left unanswered who authorized the restrictions, and why they were introduced without warning. Advertisement Partial restoration leaves Ukrainian interceptors at risk Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity was being restored at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), although restrictions on the military-grade Starshield system remained in place. Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connectivity had improved at speeds below that threshold, but the limits continued to complicate efforts to intercept Russia’s increasingly frequent jet-powered drones. One Ukrainian source said the operating speed would need to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to effectively counter the faster Russian drones.
